title: Democrats Debate Iran War Powers as Strikes Test Party Unity
description_short: After U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran, Democrats disagreed over a war-powers resolution and Israel policy, creating a test of party unity ahead of 2026 primaries.
description_medium: An Associated Press report published March 2, 2026, said U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran tested Democratic unity. Party leaders urged a war-powers vote, while Reps. Greg Landsman and Josh Gottheimer opposed the measure and Sen. John Fetterman disputed claims that the attack was illegal. The report also described disagreement over Israel and AIPAC’s role in primaries.
description_long: The Associated Press reported on March 2, 2026, that U.S. and Israeli strikes against Iran were testing a Democratic coalition that had largely opposed President Donald Trump’s immigration tactics and criticized his economic policies. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer called for a war-powers resolution to constrain the president’s options. The article reported differences within the party: Reps. Greg Landsman and Josh Gottheimer said they would not support the measure, and Sen. John Fetterman rejected arguments that the attack was illegal. It also situated the dispute in a longer debate about Israel and Gaza. AIPAC’s affiliated super PAC had opposed Tom Malinowski after he questioned unconditional aid to Israel; in New Jersey’s special primary, progressive Analilia Mejia defeated him. In Illinois, mayor Daniel Biss criticized AIPAC-aligned groups ahead of another primary. The article presented these developments as a political test, not proof of a lasting party realignment.
subcategory: Iran war and congressional war powers

title: Donald Trump’s Fordham Attendance Is Biographical Context
description_short: Trump attended Fordham for two years before transferring to Penn; this is biographical context, not a documented public act.
description_medium: Fordham’s student newspaper reported, based on alumni interviews, that Donald Trump commuted to the university’s Bronx campus for two years before transferring to the University of Pennsylvania. It also reported that a 1965 yearbook and alumni accounts place him on Fordham’s freshman squash team. The material does not establish an exact enrollment day or support the homework allegation mentioned in earlier summaries.

title: Attributed Kuchma–Derkach Conversation Mentions Mogilevich and Putin
description_short: A TrumpFile page attributes to a purported 2000 recording a conversation in which Ukrainian officials discuss Semion Mogilevich and Vladimir Putin. The page does not connect…
description_medium: TrumpFile describes a private conversation between Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma and former security-service head Leonid Derkach, said to have been recorded by security officer Mykola Melnychenko. In the excerpt, Derkach says Mogilevich was on good terms with Putin and had been in contact with him since Putin lived in Leningrad. TrumpFile attributes the material to a transcript later published by journalist J. V. Koshiw. The page does not independently authenticate the recording, and the excerpt contains no reference to Donald Trump.

title: Reported 2016 Aircraft Overlaps Involved Trump and Rybolovlev Jets
description_short: News reports describe two 2016 airport overlaps involving aircraft associated with Donald Trump’s campaign and Dmitry Rybolovlev. They do not establish that the men met or were…
description_medium: A Philadelphia Inquirer report, citing McClatchy flight records, said Rybolovlev’s aircraft landed in Las Vegas on October 30, 2016, when Trump campaigned there, and in Charlotte on November 3, near a Trump rally. It arrived in Charlotte less than an hour after Trump’s campaign plane. Rybolovlev’s representative denied contact and said the trip was for business. Aircraft timing does not establish that the men met, communicated, or were aboard together.

title: Justice Department Housing Discrimination Case Against Trump Management
description_short: In 1973, the Justice Department sued Donald Trump, Fred Trump and their company over alleged racial discrimination in rental housing. The 1975 consent decree barred…
description_medium: The Justice Department sued Donald Trump, Fred Trump and Trump Management in 1973, alleging Fair Housing Act violations. The complaint described Black applicants being denied vacancy information or steered elsewhere. The case ended in a 1975 consent decree barring discrimination and requiring training, equal-housing ads and vacancy lists for the New York Urban League. The decree expressly did not admit liability.
description_long: The Justice Department filed suit in October 1973 in the Eastern District of New York against Donald Trump, his father Fred Trump, and Trump Management, alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act across 39 buildings containing more than 14,000 apartments. The Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse case file says the complaint relied in part on paired testing: white testers were told about vacancies while Black testers were not or were steered to different properties. It also alleged employees used codes beside applicants’ names to indicate race. The defendants counterclaimed for defamation; the court dismissed that counterclaim and allowed the federal case to proceed. The parties resolved the case through a consent decree signed June 10, 1975. It barred discrimination in rental terms and practices, required Donald and Fred Trump to familiarize themselves with the Act, and required advertisements stating that minorities had equal opportunity to apply. Trump Management also had to provide the New York Urban League weekly vacancy lists for two years. The decree expressly stated that it was not an admission of a violation. The record supports the filing, allegations, and negotiated obligations, but not a claim that a court found the defendants liable.

title: Trump Proclamation Requires $100,000 Payment for Certain New H-1B Petitions
description_short: A September 2025 proclamation required a $100,000 payment with certain new H-1B petitions for workers outside the United States, effective September 21, 2025, with a…
description_medium: President Donald Trump signed the H-1B entry restriction proclamation on September 19, 2025, effective at 12:01 a.m. EDT on September 21. It required employers to document a $100,000 payment for covered petitions for workers outside the United States and gave the Homeland Security secretary discretion to grant national-interest exceptions. White House guidance said it applied to new petitions filed after the effective time, not previously issued visas or earlier petitions, and did not change renewal fees.
description_long: On September 19, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Proclamation 10973, “Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers.” It restricted entry of certain H-1B workers outside the United States unless the petition was accompanied or supplemented by a $100,000 payment, subject to exceptions. It took effect at 12:01 a.m. EDT on September 21, 2025, and assigned employers responsibility for retaining proof of payment before filing covered petitions. The text authorized the Homeland Security secretary to exempt an individual, company, or industry when hiring served the national interest and posed no security or welfare threat. White House guidance said the measure applied to new petitions submitted after the effective time, not previously issued visas or earlier petitions, and did not change renewal fees. The proclamation stated an initial 12-month period absent extension. The documented event is the entry restriction and payment condition; these sources do not establish its overall effect on hiring or visa access.

evidence_resolution.proposed_claim: The proclamation set a payment condition tied to entry by certain H-1B workers outside the U.S.; it was not a blanket fee for all applications or renewals.
